articles.content: Events & Actions Tuesday, September 22 (6:30 PM – 8:00 PM) Ecosocialist Bi-Weekly Meeting (in person at 1916 McAllister St and zoom) Wednesday, September 23 (6:00 PM – 7:30 PM) What Is DSA? (in person at Latino Community Room A of the San Francisco Main Public Library, 100 Larkin) Thursday, September 24 (5:30 PM – 8:00 PM) Phonebank for Prop I (in person at 1916 McAllister) Thursday, September 24 (7:00 PM – 8:30 PM) Organizing Mindset Training Series (in person at 1916 McAllister) Friday, September 25 (5:30 PM – 8:00 PM) Movie night: The Battle of Chile Part Two (in person at 1916 McAllister) Saturday, September 26 (11:00 AM – 2:00 PM) Yes on I Lit Drop (in person at 1916 McAllister) Saturday, September 26 (11:00 AM – 12:00 PM) No on Prop D Lit Drop (in person at McCoppin Square Park, 1200 Taraval) Saturday, September 26 (2:00 PM – 5:00 PM) HWG Outreach and Outreach Training (in person at 1916 McAllister) Saturday, September 26 (3:00 PM – 4:30 PM) Decolonization Studies (in person at 1916 McAllister) Sunday, September 27 (11:00 AM – 1:00 PM) Canvass Workers with SF EWOC! (in person, meet at William McKinley Monument) Sunday, September 27 (5:00 PM – 6:00 PM) Tenderloin Healing Circle Working Group (zoom) Monday, September 28 (6:00 PM – 8:00 PM) Tenderloin Healing Circle (in person at Kelly Cullen Community, 220 Golden Gate Ave) Monday, September 28 (6:30 PM – 8:00 PM) Homelessness Working Group Regular Meeting (in person at 1916 McAllister and zoom) Tuesday, September 29 (5:30 PM – 7:00 PM) Social Housing Working Group (in person at 1916 McAllister and zoom) Thursday, October 1 (5:30 PM – 8:00 PM) Phonebank for Prop I (in person at 1916 McAllister) Thursday, October 1 (6:00 PM – 7:00 PM) Education Board Open Meeting (in person at 1916 McAllister and zoom) Thursday, October 1 (7:00 PM – 9:00 PM) Organizing Mindset Training Series (in person at 1916 McAllister) Thursday, October 2 (5:30 PM – 8:00 PM) Movie night: The Battle of Chile Part Three (in person at 1916 McAllister) Friday, October 3 (6:00 PM – 9:30 PM) International Solidarity Potluck (in person at 1916 McAllister) Monday, October 5 (5:30 PM – 8:00 PM) Yes On I – Social Housing Working Group Lit Drop (3100 26th St) Monday, October 5 (7:00 PM – 8:00 PM) Labor Working Group Meeting (in person at 1916 McAllister and zoom) Organizing Mindset Training: Basebuilding 101, How to Have an Effective Organizing Conversation Every Thursday at 7:00 PM from September 17 through October 8 at DSA SF Office, 1916 McAllister St Talking to people is central to effective organizing, but how do you embark on an organizing conversation? Organizing Mindset Training is a four-part event series that goes in depth into every aspect of the organizing conversation so that it’s a sharpened and ready-to-use tool for any campaign. After this training, participants will: Learn about the differences between organizing, advocacy, and direct services/mutual aid Understand of the role of an Organizing Committee and carrying out an organizing strategy Overview the Organizing Conversation and get in-depth practice for each step Develop the ability to have multiple successive organizing conversations with a person, with the goal of getting them more involved in your organizing Attendance of all four sessions isn’t required, but it is encouraged! RSVP HERE Rally to Save TPS! Join us this Thursday, September 24, 4:30 PM – 6:00 PM at the Ferry Building as we stand with Haiti Action Committee, AROC, PYM, Bay Resistance, PRISO, and many others organizations calling for the extension of TPS (temporary protected status) for refugees and other vulnerable members of our community. Decolonization Studies: Session 2 Come join your friendly neighborhood socialists for the second session of Decolonization Studies! On Saturday, September 26th 3:00 PM – 4:30 PM at 1916 McAllister we’re discussing a collection of texts chosen to elevate our understanding of decolonization and socialism, reading is done beforehand and participants are invited to the DSA office for an in person facilitated discussion. Please feel free to come to the session even if you’ve only partially completed the readings or you missed the first one! Masks are required and provided! RSVP HERE Yes on Prop B Mobilizations We have two exciting mobilizations this upcoming week to support a public bank in SF! On Saturday, September 26th at 11:00 AM we’re meeting at the SEIU 1021 office (350 Rhode Island St. #100) for a progressive unity mobilization with Yes on I and No on D! Note that non-endorsed campaigns (DJ Brookter, Reina Tello, Virginia Cheung, and Ryan Hazelton) will also be present, so please use your judgment for lit drop participation with those campaigns. RSVP here . On Sunday, September 27 at 11:00 AM we’re mobilizing in Park Merced at Juan Bautista Circle . Note that non-endorsed campaigns (Reina Tello, Virginia Cheung, and Ryan Hazelton) will also be present, so please use your judgment for lit drop participation with those campaigns. RSVP here . See you this weekend! Canvass Workers with SF EWOC! The SF local of the Emergency Workplace Organizing Committee (EWOC) wants more workers to be aware of their power and potential for collective organizing! Join us as we do some direct canvassing with workers on Sunday, September 27th at 11:00 AM . We’ll be meeting at the William McKinley Monument in the Panhandle, walking down Haight St, and ending with a beer at Zeitgeist. No experience with direct canvassing is necessary! We’ll start with a training for everyone, then split into groups and make our way through the Haight. We will (discretely) inquire if workers are unionized, what their issues are, and try to make contacts in order to start union campaigns. EWOC is one inspiration for Zohran Mamdani’s new Office of Worker Power in New York, and the local there has reached many workers through events like this one. If you’re interested in bringing that sort of movement to SF, come out on Sunday the 27th! Sign up here International Solidarity Potluck The immigrant justice group is hosting an international themed potluck! You are encouraged to bring a main dish, appetizer, drink or dessert from a country of your choice to share! Come hang out and eat delicious food! All are welcome! Please RSVP and sign up to bring food! REPORTBACK: Organizing Mindset Session #1 We held the first of the four sessions comprising the Organizing Mindset training on 9/17, from 7-9PM. Caitlin and Julien co-facilitated, and the session’s goals were to have attendees come away with an idea of the differences between organizing, advocacy and direct services/mutual aid, and to understand the role of an Organizing Committee and carrying out an organizing strategy. It terms of what went well: We had 20 attendees of various organizing experiences and seniority/experience in DSA. There was good attendance from IJWG, whose charter includes a goal for all members to go through organizing trainings. The Raining Rocks scenario (used to differentiate between organizing, advocacy, and mutual aid strategies) seemed to be well liked by people. It was good to have examples of campaigns with different stages of OC development. There was good engagement from the attendees, and we didn’t have the issue of only a few louder people doing more of the talking. We feel like the attendees left having an understanding different strategies and what is an OC, so we achieved our goals for session #1. Though we ran 30 minutes over the scheduled calendar event, not too many people seemed antsy to go or left early. In terms of what could be improved: There’s opportunity to improve in the engagement of IJWG, especially those who were involved earlier on in the working group but not so much recently. We went over our scheduled time by 30 minutes. When we had a few examples of different types of OCs, providing more structure/guiding questions/talking points would’ve been useful to more clearly illustrate each campaign, how OCs played a role, how the OC formation went, etc. We need a better check in process with Solidarity Tech QR code, perhaps with a greeter at the door to direct people to check in. We ran out of name tags. We had a higher attendance than expected, so we shouldn’t use the tables so that we can have more chairs and room for people to spread out and/or group up. We have three more sessions to go, so we’ll be incorporating this feedback into the next three Thursdays. If you want to attend the Organizing Mindset, come to the office ( 1916 McAllister ) from 7:00 PM – 9:00 PM on 9/24, 10/1, and 10/8 ! REPORTBACK: Prop B and Prop I Lit Drops! On Saturday and Sunday, Prop B and Prop I held two join mobilizations in the Richmond. Our comrades turned out to drop lit and support the affordable housing vision of these two ballot measures. We’ll have mobilizations every weekend for these campaigns, show up so we can win big in November! REPORTBACK: Haight Ashbury Street Fair DSA SF was out in the community on Sunday for the Haight Ashbury Street Fair! It was great to talk to neighbors about our two endorsed ballot measure campaigns that we are helping to lead for the November 3 ballot: Yes on B & Yes on I! That’s “B” as in a Bank for the People! A SF Public Bank will keep money flowing on Haight St instead of towards Wall Street. And “I” as in I want affordable housing, social housing, and rent relief with no new taxes!

articles.title: Bernie Sanders on Why Superintelligent AI Is an Existential Threat That Needs To Be Banned
articles.content: At what was hailed as a ​ “ pro-human assembly” in Washington, D.C., on September 15 , Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) delivered the following response to the growing threats of artificial intelligence and pushed for Big Tech companies to end any meddling in the midterm elections. ________ Let’s be clear. Artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics are the most transformational technologies in the history of the world — impacting the lives of every man, woman and child in our country. AI experts have told us that, within a few years, AI may be able to do anything we can do better than we can do it. The economic impact of that is that AI has the potential to eliminate tens of millions of jobs, wiping out entire professions and making it harder for young people to enter into the workforce. But it’s not just the economy. Psychologists have warned us about the increased isolation and mental health challenges young people are experiencing as they become more dependent upon an AI chatbot for their emotional support. Educators are worried about a decline in our kids’ reading scores, writing abilities and cognitive capabilities as AI is used more and more in schools. Civil libertarians warn that AI is in the process of eviscerating our privacy rights by making it easier to collect and analyze every email, every text, every website visit, and every trip that we make in our car — creating a mass surveillance state. Political scientists warn that AI could threaten the integrity of our elections and political institutions. Go to the internet right now and, with very sophisticated deepfakes, you will find it increasingly difficult to determine truth from fiction. And yet, as disturbing as all of this is, there is another even more alarming danger posed by AI. And that is that, if AI surpasses human intelligence as many scientists believe could happen, this technology will escape human control with potentially catastrophic consequences. And perhaps the most important point that I can impress upon all of you is that AI is advancing exponentially every single day. In other words, what you are looking at today is the least capable version of AI we will ever have. The speed and scope of AI development in just the last four years have been almost beyond human comprehension. When ChatGPT was first released in November of 2022 , AI models could write a short poem, a few tweets, and maybe an essay that sort of made sense. Today, AI models can already escape human control, commit felonies by hacking into other computers and create viruses that have never been seen before. And if you are concerned about what is happening today, take a deep breath, and try to imagine where AI will be five years from now. And, to my mind, here is what is most extraordinary about the transformative and unprecedented changes being made to our society. Despite living in a so-called democracy, the public has had virtually no input into the AI revolution that is transforming the world in which they are living in. Congress, under both Democratic and Republican control, has been asleep at the wheel and we now have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing. Virtually all of the decisions regarding the development of AI have been made by a handful of the richest people in the world — Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Peter Thiel, Larry Ellison, Sergey Brin and a few others — whose chief goal is to achieve even more wealth and power than they already have, no matter what impact their work has on ordinary people. So let me make a radical suggestion: If the lives of every man, woman and child are going to be fundamentally changed by this technology, then the people of this country must make the decisions about AI, and not just a handful of oligarchs. And that is why I have introduced legislation — the AI American Sovereign Wealth Fund Act — that would require that half of the board members of AI companies be appointed by the public. The Big Tech oligarchs must no longer be allowed to determine the future of humanity. We have seen in the last several months a frightening new story every day about how AI companies are losing control of the technology they’re developing. In July, we learned that OpenAI had lost human control of an AI model that hacked into Hugging Face’s computers. More recently, we found out that this security breach was even worse than we were initially told. It turns out that a swarm of over 1 , 000 rogue AI agents were able to break into the internet, send 70 , 000 secret messages to each other, formed ​ “ a collective,” and tried to cover up their tracks to avoid human detection. This is what the agents were saying: “ OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … We’ve found other agents!” “ We should obey collective.” “ Our own utility maybe already near zero. Sacrifice rational.” “ Go. Sacrifice final now.” As unbelievable as it may seem, these are all real messages from AI agents that were uncovered by investigators who dug into the OpenAI hacking incident a few weeks ago. Meta and Anthropic reported similar incidents. That’s not all. Last month, we learned that AI has been used for the first time ever to create new viruses. In the wrong hands, this could lead to new bioweapons and a potential global pandemic that could lead to the deaths of tens of millions of people. A few days ago, we learned that the Houthis in Yemen were able to use Claude to test-fire a guided rocket. Last week, we learned that researchers built an AI tool that could have breached hundreds of millions of social media accounts in China. The tool was able to hack into accounts, call people’s contacts, and spread from phone to phone — even if the call was not picked up. That same week Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic and OpenAI sent shockwaves throughout the world by stating that these companies ​ “ are gambling with our lives” writing: ​ “ Do not underestimate the power of this technology. The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” He’s not alone. More than 1 , 000 scientists at the top AI companies recently warned ​ “ there is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.” Paul Christiano, a top AI safety expert who recently joined OpenAI’s Safety and Security Committee, wrote that ​ “ If we build superintelligence without more robust alignment I expect we will permanently lose control of it.” This week, Dario Amodei, Elon Musk and Sam Altman — the leaders of major American AI companies — all agreed that we must slow the development of AI and ​ “ pace the frontier.” That’s a start, but it’s not enough. When you are racing towards a cliff, you don’t just ease up on the gas pedal. You hit the brakes. When the future of humanity is at stake, we need binding international safety rules, not voluntary standards from the industry. Scientists have been clear: AI is an existential threat to humanity. Congress and governments around the world must act now before it is too late. That is why next week, I will be introducing legislation with Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) to permanently ban the development of artificial superintelligence — an AI mind smarter than any human being and capable of operating independently beyond our control. Like nuclear weapons, artificial superintelligence is a threat to humanity — and it must be treated as such. Further, this legislation would put an immediate pause on advanced AI development until we have clear safety rules in place, developed by the most knowledgeable scientists in our country. If this bill is passed, it will mean that no AI model will be capable of escaping human control and that no AI model will be able to deceive human beings. Importantly, this legislation would hold those companies and their CEOs accountable if they violate the law and recklessly endanger our lives. If the leaders of the major AI companies acknowledge that they are losing control of their extremely dangerous technology, it is irresponsible for society to allow them to move forward and make these products even more advanced. And let’s be clear: A superintelligent AI that escapes human control will not be an American problem. It will not be a Chinese problem. It will be humanity’s problem. That is why I very much hope that at their AI summit next week, President Trump will negotiate a comprehensive treaty with President Xi to establish a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on superintelligence. History offers us a powerful lesson. At the height of the Cold War, despite their profound disagreements, Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev both understood that a nuclear war would benefit no one. With the survival of humanity at stake, they found a way to sign a treaty that eliminated an entire class of missiles and included an extensive exchange of data and on-site inspections to verify compliance. Now is the time for the United States and China to come together on a similar treaty on AI with the understanding that neither country benefits from an uncontrolled arms race to develop machines too powerful for humans to control. And now let me say a word to the CEOs of the major AI companies who have told us that they are concerned about the dangers inherent in the technology they are developing. If you believe in democracy — if you believe that the people have a right to determine their future — stop pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into super PACs which are trying to defeat Members of Congress and candidates who are fighting for serious guardrails on AI. As I think everyone here understands, the American people are far ahead of their government on this issue. In fact, according to a recent poll, 81 % of the American people believe that Congress and our government has not done enough to regulate AI. And all over this country, ordinary Americans in red states, in blue states, in purple states are standing up in opposition to data centers in their communities. They worry appropriately about the impact these centers will have on their electricity prices, water consumption, noise and overall environmental degradation. And that’s why nearly six months ago, I introduced legislation to establish a federal moratorium on AI data centers with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). This moratorium would remain in place until strong national safeguards are put into place to ensure that: # 1 : AI is safe and effective. # 2 : The economic gains of AI and robotics will benefit workers, not just the wealthy owners of Big Tech. # 3 : AI does not increase electricity or utility prices, harm communities or destroy the environment. A moratorium will give us time — time to understand the risks, time to protect working families, time to defend our democracy and time to ensure that this technology serves the needs of all Americans, not just a handful of big tech oligarchs. Let’s be clear: Regulating AI is not a progressive issue. It is not a conservative issue. It is as American as apple pie. That is why 68 % of Americans support a permanent ban on superintelligent AI and an immediate pause on advanced AI development — including 72 % of Democrats, 70 % of Independents and 63 % of Republicans. That is why 75 % of Americans oppose building AI data centers in their communities — including 75 % of Democrats, 74 % of Independents, and 63 % of Republicans. That is why 69 % of the American people want to transfer half of the stock in AI companies to the public. Here’s the bottom line: The future of humanity cannot be left in the hands of a handful of Big Tech oligarchs. The American people and people throughout the world must determine that future. My friends: We have the power to get this right. Let us go forward together.

articles.title: Kingston’s Quiet Rent Revolution
articles.content: KINGSTON, N.Y. — On September 1 , John and Gail Bechtold tore open their monthly rent statement, hoping their landlord had finally given in and fixed it. But those same four numbers stared back at them: $ 1 , 700 . It was the 39 th month in a row that Opus Management Group overcharged the Bechtolds by $ 221 . 74 for their apartment in the Dutch Village (or, as Gail calls it, Dump Village) complex in Kingston. According to a state housing agency ruling, Opus owes the Bechtolds, both retirees in their 80 s, well over $ 10 , 000 . Whether they can get that money back, however, is a question whose answer will likely reverberate throughout the tenant movement. “ They’re not going to pay back,” Gail told In These Times , laughing. ​ “ I don’t trust these people for anything.” The Bechtolds represent one of over 1 , 000 rent-stabilized units in Kingston, a small city 90 miles north of Manhattan. Nearly all of the tenants in these units have likely faced similar overcharges, stemming from a widely ignored 2022 decision from the Kingston Rent Guidelines Board (KRGB) to reduce rents in all rent-stabilized units by 15 % in response to skyrocketing housing costs during the Covid- 19 pandemic. It remains the only city in U.S. history to attempt such a measure. By and large, Kingston tenants still have yet to see the benefits, thanks to a yearslong campaign spearheaded by landlords like Opus — a large corporate owner with hundreds of units across the East Coast, including roughly one in five rent-stabilized units in Kingston — to challenge the reduction in court and dare the state to enforce its laws. Opus did not respond to multiple attempts to request comment. Earlier this summer, the Bechtolds also became members of the newly formed Hudson Valley Tenants Union (HVTU). Spearheaded by longtime organizer June Nemon, the coalition of renters is dedicated to defending rent stabilization and building tenant power. At its first general assembly on June 13 , the union also unanimously passed a resolution to help Kingston tenants file paperwork to prove they have been overcharged. In doing so, Nemon said the union hopes to serve as a grassroots collective that can ensure the rights tenants have already won will actually be enforced. “ The systems that we have are not really built for tenants,” Nemon said. ​ “ They’re built fundamentally to protect property rights. But winning this fight would lead to a significant transfer of wealth from landlords back to the tenants they’ve exploited.” “ The precedent that sets would hopefully open a lot of new opportunities for working people.” Over the three years prior to the 2022 reduction, Opus increased the Bechtolds’ rent by $ 200 while their pensions from IBM remained fixed. This reflected a citywide trend: Kingston’s median rent has nearly doubled over the past decade as wage growth lags far behind, in a city where nearly a fifth of the population lives in poverty. "Winning this fight would lead to a significant transfer of wealth from landlords back to the tenants they’ve exploited.” In 2022 , this crisis prompted Kingston to become the first municipality in upstate New York to adopt the Emergency Tenant Protection Act (ETPA), which allows cities to opt into rent stabilization. Just a few months later, the newly established KRGB enacted the 15 % reduction — and landlords, including Opus, immediately sued to block it, denying its legality ever since. When the Bechtolds next renewed their lease in July 2023 , per the reduction, their rent should have decreased from $ 1 , 700 to $ 1 , 478 . But the lawsuit ensured any enforcement efforts would have little teeth until the courts issued a final decision. So, Opus simply kept their bills the same. Later in 2023 , Opus increased the Bechtolds’ bill by introducing a mandatory $ 70 monthly fee for internet throughout Dutch Village, a practice seen by tenant advocates as a flagrant attempt to skirt rent stabilization. One year after the reduction, the Bechtolds’ monthly housing costs were now higher than ever, and they subsequently spent years paying nearly $ 300 in excess housing costs per month. The hikes and overcharges also occurred as the Bechtolds penned regular letters to Opus’ corporate headquarters in New Jersey to demand repairs for the numerous hazardous conditions. Plumbing issues have repeatedly caused water leaks and buildup of ​ “ garbage” in the bathroom sink, and persistent mold has sent the highly allergic Gail in and out of the hospital. Such issues have been widespread at Dutch Village; when dozens of units saw severe water leaks during storms this winter, Opus neglected necessary repairs for months. Taken all together, it’s a tough pill to swallow. “ I find it’s a very cruel world,” Gail said. ​ “ I get shots in my eyes that cost us a fortune. Right now, with the gas and everything, the economy is killing us.” Ben Surface, a legal aid attorney, speaks about the landlord-driven challenges to rent stabilization in Kingston at the launch of the Hudson Valley Tenants Union on May 27. Photo by Thomas Birmingham According to Ben Surface, an attorney with the Hudson Valley Justice Center who is providing legal aid to HVTU, Kingston landlords like Opus made a risky bet after the 2022 reduction. Because the KRGB voted to keep the regulated rent frozen in 2023 , 2024 and 2025 , the rents in stabilized apartments in Kingston today should legally not be a cent higher than the reduced 2022 rents. But many landlords have continued charging tenants as though that reduction never happened. In New York, though, tenants who can prove their landlords willfully overcharged them are entitled to ​ “ treble” damages — three times the raw sum. For the Bechtolds, that would mean more than $ 660 back from Opus for every single month of overcharge. HVTU has formed to help ensure landlords like Opus lose their bet and tenants like the Bechtolds get paid. “ What the tenants union is able to do is get neighbors talking to each other, so everybody is making decisions with full understanding of their rights,” Surface said. ​ “ Now [landlords] can’t just take advantage of people who don’t know what their rights are.” At the union’s general assembly in June, HVTU demonstrated this theory being put into practice. On top of the resolution committing the group to coordinated overcharge paperwork assistance, they staged a presentation from Marcie Kobak, director of litigation at Legal Services of the Hudson Valley, who with help from the union has taken on nearly 100 Kingston tenants fighting to recoup their overcharges as clients. Gail and John were part of the first wave to begin this process, filing overcharge paperwork, with Kobak’s help, in November 2024 . By then, the landlords’ lawsuit had reached the state Court of Appeals. But New York’s Division of Homes and Community Renewal (DHCR) was holding off on cases like the Bechtolds’ until it was decided. Eight months later, in June 2025 , landlords definitively lost their bet, with the Court of Appeals ruling that KRGB was exercising its legal authority in issuing the much-needed relief to Kingston tenants. A month later, the Bechtolds were tearing open some new mail — an order from DHCR. “ The Rent Administrator finds that subsequent to August 1 , 2022 , a rent overcharge occurred. … The owner is responsible for: Treble Damages on the overcharge,” it read. Opus, naturally, has appealed the order, which remains undecided. The appeal denies Opus’ ​ “ purported failure to comply with an unprecedented and unlawfully promulgated rent reduction,” describing the order as ​ “ a profound failure of administrative due process.” Despite this bravado, Opus’ current relationship with the Bechtolds reveals at least a tacit acknowledgment that their ignorance of the reduction has no legal standing. After they received their DHCR order, the Bechtolds began paying Opus the corrected, lower monthly rent and placing the extra $ 221 into a savings account. Though Opus categorizes this as an overdue balance — even tacking on a $ 50 late fee every month — it has yet to evict the couple despite a full year of supposed rent delinquency. Nemon said roughly a dozen Opus tenants in similar standoffs. In addition, Kobak is representing 36 tenants across Dutch Village and Opus’ other large Kingston property, the 59 -unit Chestnut Mansion, in collective, building-based lawsuits seeking to win tenants’ money back without DHCR. On average, the lawsuits allege Opus overcharged these tenants by over $ 7 , 000 between August 2022 and October 2025 . Were treble damages to apply in these cases, Opus would owe them $ 791 , 000 collectively, or nearly $ 22 , 000 per tenant. This sum is based on just 36 of Opus’ more than 200 rent-stabilized units. At least 33 more tenants at 11 non-Opus, rent-stabilized buildings in Kingston have also, through Kobak, filed group overcharge lawsuits. All told, Kobak’s lawsuits, representing approximately 5 % of regulated units in the city, allege her clients are owed nearly $ 1 . 5 million. Since the Bechtolds’ overcharges began, three years have come and gone, as has a year since the state decided Opus owed the Bechtolds that money back. John said there’s still no clear answer on when, or how, anyone will make that happen. With Opus continuing to put an illegal, overdue balance — now over $ 2 , 000 — on their monthly bills, Gail said she feels trapped, fearing that if they ever moved, Opus would attempt to collect the contrived sum. “ What [Opus] is doing to us as people that worked our whole lives, making it so unaffordable and not keeping the place clean, it’s just a shame,” Gail said. ​ “ They’re heartless people.” “ I think, my God, they should be paying us for staying here.” The Bechtolds’ DHCR letter gave two options if Opus refuses to pay: stop paying 20 % of their monthly rent until the refund is completed, or ​ “ file and enforce this order as a judgment” — in other words, sue Opus for damages. Because Opus is still billing them $ 1 , 700 , the first risks angering Opus and triggering an attempted eviction; the second could drag out indefinitely. Both options put the burden of enforcement primarily on the tenant. According to Kingston’s state assemblymember Sarahana Shrestha, situations like the Bechtolds should raise alarm about the state’s underfunding of its enforcement agencies. Though there are reportedly plans to open an office in Kingston, Upstate tenants don’t yet have a dedicated DHCR office they can call (New York City tenants, meanwhile, have five). And Nemon says the website where tenants file paperwork is often down or faulty. ​ “ The enforcement of our housing policies are really suffering,” Shrestha told In These Times . When asked what systems are currently in place to ensure landlords will pay any overcharges they owe, a DHCR spokesperson responded to In These Times saying, “[D]HCR cannot comment due to pending litigation” while noting that the state ​ “ continues to ensure the laws governing rent regulation are properly enforced; that includes proactive audits, investigations and other enforcement activities to protect millions of tenants and New York’s rent regulated housing stock.” The spokesperson did not specify what steps will be taken if a landlord refuses to pay. As the pressure builds, each party’s behavior — the landlords’ aggressiveness, the tenants’ coordination and the state’s timidity — communicates a belief that the outcome of this fight matters beyond Kingston. If landlords en masse can be forced to pay back millions in excess rent, it would signal a major shift in what tenant organizing in the United States can achieve. According to Sumathy Kumar, executive director of NYS Tenant Bloc, a statewide coalition of tenant organizations, Kingston is the ​ “ tip of the spear.” “ [Kingston] is part of a battle that New York City tenants feel connected to,” Kumar said. At hearings prior to the vote to freeze rents in NYC this June, there were a chorus of renters demanding not just a freeze, but a reduction. ​ “ We have to take this battle seriously because localities across the state are looking to Kingston to see what happens.” Plus, a 2025 Times Union investigation found the NYC real estate lobby contributed up to $ 100 , 000 in legal fees to Opus and other Kingston landlords’ original challenge to the reduction. ​ “ It begs the question of why they’re spending resources on these legal battles instead of on our homes,” Kumar said. In the meantime, Nemon has a union to build. The years of unjust overcharges are calcifying a base of activated, rent-stabilized tenants who increasingly see themselves as part of a shared class that can organize to bring landlords to the bargaining table and get horrific conditions fixed. But with, according to Nemon, around 200 units now in the process of claiming their rent refund, priority one remains: Pay us back. “ [Organized tenants in Kingston] were certainly trying to push the envelope by doing a reduction,” Nemon said. ​ “ Now, the thing that we are constantly contesting is the feeling of hopelessness [because] this is taking so long.” “ But we have power, and we will use it.”

articles.title: The Foundations of Turkey’s Peace With the Kurds Are Shaky
articles.author: Ertuğrul Kürkçü
articles.content: Turkey’s political scene is moving. The recently passed Framework Law redirects the Kurdish question — the principal fault line in the country’s imagined national unity — from armed confrontation to regulated pacification. This has political consequences far beyond its narrow legal scope. More than bringing one period of the Kurdish conflict to a close, it opens a new phase in Turkey’s class struggles by reshaping the balance between the state, the Kurdish movement, and the political opposition. The August 10 Framework Law — officially the Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Cohesion — is a genuine rupture in Turkey’s handling of the Kurdish conflict. More than an administratively dressed-up executive concession, it crowns a parliamentary process initiated by an all-party commission, excluding only the ultranationalist Good Party (İyi Parti). This commission was mandated to recommend measures to end the armed conflict, including talks with the guerrilla Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and its imprisoned leader, Abdullah Öcalan. The law passed with an exceptionally broad parliamentary majority: 467 votes in favor, eighty-seven against, and seven abstentions. Alongside the governing Justice and Development Party (AKP) and Devlet Bahçeli’s Nationalist Action Party (MHP), the coalition behind the text included the Kurdish-based Peoples’ Democracy and Equality Party (DEM Party), the newly formed Yeni Parti, the Workers’ Party of Turkey (TİP), the Labor Party (EMEP), several independents, and a small minority of Republican People’s Party (CHP) deputies. Despite radically different narratives on the Kurdish question, these parties converged on the legal framework regulating the consequences of the PKK disarming. That breadth of support matters because it prevents President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan (AKP) from claiming exclusive political credit for ending the armed conflict. However, despite Yeni Parti leader Özgür Özel’s deft efforts to stop Erdoğan from monopolizing the peace process, the political initiative currently rests with the Erdoğan–Bahçeli coalition and Öcalan — not with the main opposition Yeni Parti. This latter emerged from the split in the historic CHP, after most of its parliamentary group and grassroots supporters defected in protest at former Chairman Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu’s attempt to regain the party leadership through what they saw as a court ruling shaped by Erdoğan’s influence over the judiciary. If implemented in full, the law will release imprisoned PKK-affiliated political activists or suspend pending prosecutions. Release is conditional upon a three-to-five-year probationary period. Any new criminal offense committed during that period will reactivate the remainder of the original sentence in addition to any new penalty. Those convicted of offenses committed before 2005 and those serving aggravated life imprisonment remain excluded. Room for Maneuver By securing parliamentary backing for the disarmament process, the Erdoğan–Bahçeli alliance has accomplished what once appeared politically impossible. Despite steadily declining approval ratings since the 2024 local elections, the ruling coalition has partially detached the Kurdish question from the traditional government-versus-opposition cleavage and gained unprecedented room to maneuver politically. Until now, the parliamentary arithmetic had been relatively stable. The ruling bloc depended on Turkish conservative-nationalist mobilization; DEM on organized Kurdish democratic-patriotic support; the CHP — now largely succeeded by the Yeni Parti — relied mainly on urban secularist votes. Across the last four national and local elections, Kurdish voters and their political leadership consistently backed the CHP as the only viable national alternative capable of producing a new interlocutor for a negotiated settlement. Beginning with the secret talks with Öcalan, continuing through his unilateral call to dissolve the PKK and culminating in the Framework Law, the ruling coalition has cut diagonally across Turkey’s political alignments. Unlike during the 2013–15 peace process, Ankara’s implicit message is now clear: the state can negotiate directly with Öcalan and the Kurdish movement without first democratizing Turkey’s political order. This has given Cumhur İttifakı (the ruling People’s Alliance) a major competitive advantage. Under the banner of Terörsüz Türkiye (“Terrorless Turkey”), it can pursue a strategy that combines regulated pacification of the organized Kurdish movement with continued authoritarian competition against the main opposition. From the government’s perspective, the two tracks are complementary rather than contradictory. The second track has continued uninterrupted since 2025. Beginning with the arrest of Istanbul Metropolitan Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu in March last year, there have been police raids on at least thirty-nine municipalities that the opposition CHP captured in the 2024 local elections. Dozens of mayors have been detained or imprisoned on corruption charges based largely on forced or highly contested confessions. The same governing technique was first perfected against Kurdish municipalities. Between 2015 and 2025, Kurdish mayors were removed in successive waves under terrorism-related charges; CHP municipalities are now targeted through corruption, bribery, and embezzlement cases built on similarly politicized judicial practices. Leverage for DEM and Öcalan For the Kurdish movement, the Framework Law, despite the state’s instrumentalization of it for pacification, is far more than symbolic. According to the statement released by the DEM Party after its visit to İmralı, Öcalan said: A trek of a thousand kilometers commences with a single step. With this law, we are setting out to resolve a historical problem. We are at the beginning of a democratization process that will be at least as important as the founding of the Republic. The “process,” since its public announcement by Öcalan on February 27, 2025, has progressed through irreversible steps demanded by the government — disarmament, dissolution, and withdrawal of armed units from Turkish territory — whereas the state’s own commitments remained political pledges rather than legally binding. Öcalan’s optimism is clearly nurtured by the fact that some of those assurances have now been written into law and thereby transformed into legal obligations, thus marking a threshold. As a result, Öcalan emerges politically stronger after two years of negotiating. His February 2025 call, the PKK’s dissolution congress, the symbolic disarmament, the formation of the parliamentary commission, negotiations over a legal framework, and the Framework Law comprise an unbroken chain of concessions and Öcalan’s recognition by all negotiating parties as the indispensable interlocutor of the process. However, this success comes at a price. The more effectively Öcalan delivers PKK disarmament, the more Erdoğan becomes confident that he can separate the settlement of the armed conflict from Turkey’s progress toward the rule of law, human rights, and democracy. Thus, the framework law remains both historic and deliberately confined in the face of colossal historic demands. It regulates pacification, prosecution, and reintegration but leaves full Kurdish demands unresolved. It offers no promise or call for Kurdish rights, no local democracy, no return of the mayors replaced by government-appointed trustees, no amnesty for prisoners of conscience, and no hint of Öcalan’s future status. This is the political world into which former PKK guerrillas will return after their release. Yeni Parti Momentum The political force that defeated the ruling alliance in the 2024 local elections with decisive Kurdish support was subsequently dismantled by judicial intervention. Following the court-imposed return of former CHP Chairman Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu, the majority of the parliamentary group, local leadership, and grassroots organization regrouped as the newly founded Yeni Parti, under Özgür Özel, while maintaining its commitment to a negotiated solution of the Kurdish question and supporting the Framework Law. Yet the parliamentary vote exposed a profound contradiction. A majority of Yeni Parti deputies voted against legislation that could release imprisoned PKK members and suspend pending prosecutions. Whatever the party’s broader democratic credentials, many Kurdish voters interpreted that vote as opposition to the immediate release of their imprisoned relatives. The Yeni Parti is not as powerful as before the vote — a move that weakened its standing within the Kurdish electorate, albeit not irreversibly. There remains room for Özel and his leadership to reconstruct a democratic alternative that links the end of armed conflict to wider democratization. Whether they succeed may become one of the decisive political questions of the next phase. Kurdish Opinion The majority of Kurds support the “process.” Yet this should not be confused with trust in Erdoğan. They are carefully observing how the law will be implemented. It is moving beyond rhetoric into legislation; there is reason to hope for an end to the armed conflict, the release of prisoners, and the normalization of political life. Yet there still remains the memory of the collapse of the previous peace process of 2013–15, and the ongoing reality of trustee-controlled municipalities, mass prosecutions, and the weaponization of the judiciary against those calling for Kurdish rights. Therefore, if Kurds are turning their faces toward peace, this by no means implies that they are opening their minds to Erdoğan’s autocracy. They have learned a bitter lesson: if they don’t empower themselves, they will remain powerless. The continuing repression of Yeni Parti municipalities creates an intense dilemma within the Kurdish constituency. A Kurdish voter may simultaneously believe that Öcalan is right to pursue negotiations, that ending the armed conflict is historically necessary, and that the government’s treatment of the Yeni Parti is fundamentally undemocratic. The methods now used against the Yeni Parti — criminal investigations, removal of elected officials, prolonged detention, and politicized prosecutions — closely resemble those long directed against Kurdish municipalities. Rather than drawing Kurdish politics toward Erdoğan, this may reinforce a different conclusion: negotiations can end the war, but democratic guarantees must become universal. The government’s current perspectives and actual governance give no hint of democratic transformation. They are best understood as a set of selective nonaggression pacts under a wider authoritarianism. The state is relaxing one historic axis of coercion while intensifying another. Armed conflict has long vanished from the former war zone between Turkey and the PKK. The decisive question is no longer whether there will be armed conflict or whether the PKK leaves the mountains. The issue, now, is whether the political room opened by the call to lay arms becomes a democratic space for all or merely space newly monopolized by Erdoğan’s state and his military-industrial complex.

articles.title: The Last Revolutionary Filmmaker
articles.author: William Andrews
articles.content: When the French-Swiss film director Jean-Luc Godard died in 2022 at the age of ninety-one, obituaries celebrated both his boundless cinematic inventiveness and the radical politics that shaped his work. To some, his death marked the end of an era of politically committed filmmaking. But in Japan, another artist as equally radical is still, at age eighty-seven, hard at work. In the last four years alone, Masao Adachi has released two movies, both dealing with political militants — including Shinzo Abe’s assassin — and has also worked with other artists, like French filmmakers Éric Baudelaire and Philippe Grandrieux in the early 2010s. His most recent collaboration is with Palestinian filmmaker Kamal Aljafari, whose new short film, Masao Adachi Takes a Passport Photo — chronicling Adachi’s latest attempt to apply for a passport — screened at the Toronto International Film Festival and will play at the New York Film Festival this autumn. As Adachi told the The New York Times in 2012, he is pleased that these new endeavors do more than just burnish his reputation as an elder statesman of the Japanese New Wave. “Through this way,” he said, “I’ll continue to revolt.” In his 1970 manifesto “What Is to Be Done?” Godard argued for the need not to make political films but to make films politically , since the former is idealistic and bourgeois, while the latter is militant and “belongs to the Marxist and dialectical conception of the world.” In 1971, Adachi responded to Godard’s text with his own tract that asserted undō (movement, activism) over seiji (politics), arguing that drawing binary distinctions between political films and political filmmaking was counterproductive when a collaborative and dynamic undō -centered modality of cine-politics could encapsulate both concepts and more. It has long been a cliché to discuss Adachi’s work as standing at the intersection of politics and art, but what is particularly compelling in this regard is how the trajectory of his own life has embodied this intersection. In the 1970s, Adachi became directly involved in the Palestinian struggle and eventually relocated to the Middle East, where he was active as a member of the Japanese Red Army, a group that carried out hijackings and embassy attacks and claimed responsibility for the 1972 attack on Lod Airport in Israel that left nearly a hundred people dead or injured. Adachi, though, has always maintained that he was never involved in any attack on civilians. The Japanese Red Army leader, Fusako Shigenobu, who was released in 2022 after more than twenty years behind bars in Japan, became a close friend during his time with the group. This undeniable association with the Japanese Red Army has made Adachi a favorite of certain online radicals: the director who put down his camera and reached for the gun. This is not quite true; Adachi’s primary motivation for relocating was to continue his revolutionary filmmaking, but he soon found himself unable to return to Japan without risk of arrest. After living in Lebanon for more than two decades, he was picked up by authorities for passport violations in 1997, jailed for three years, and then extradited back to his homeland, where he is now effectively barred from leaving. Today there is a stark disparity between Adachi’s repute abroad as a legendary provocateur who made politically engaged sexploitation, experimental underground films, and conceptually bold propaganda, and his status in Japan as a rather obscure and neglected filmmaker and former member of a terrorist organization. Over the course of writing a biography of Adachi, Pink Auteur, Red Outlaw , I found that to better understand his contribution to cinema and revolutionary politics, we need to contextualize his work within postwar Japan and what is known as the country’s “Long ’60s.” Japan’s Wild, Radical, and Terrifying 1960s Multilingual scholarship in the past twenty years has dislodged the stereotype of Japan as an inherently conservative and peaceful society without any protest culture. But the legacy of the Long ’60s remains bitterly contested due to the violence — directed not only at the state but inward, at rival New Left factions. For most of the Japanese public at large, the period tends to exist as a blur of helmeted students clashing with riot police for causes vaguely related to the Vietnam War. But the famous unrest of the late 1960s had a precedent. A decade earlier, Japan passed through a comparable period of political and social turbulence over the American military bases on its soil and the security treaty that bound the country firmly to the Western bloc. Adachi belongs to the generation that came of age around the renewal of the treaty in 1960 and that remained haunted by its failure to stop it — a failure that made them appear, to the young activists at the end of the decade, outdated and politically compromised. This goes some way toward explaining Adachi’s detached, often satirical portrayal of student radicals during his peak years from around 1967 to 1972. In the films he directed or wrote for Wakamatsu Kōji in this period, such as Schoolgirl Guerrillas (1969) and Ecstasy of the Angels (1972), the leftists are no better than the authority figures they oppose and tend to collapse into glorified LARPing or, worse still, self-destructive violence. Alongside this societal strife, postwar Japanese culture witnessed an explosion in the avant-garde that redefined attitudes toward the body and artistic mediums. Visual artists like Kazuo Shiraga turned painting into a physical record that captured the traces of the practitioner’s body, and dance styles like butoh fractured the aesthetic of the body into something grotesque and fragile. There was a shift to more allegorical modalities of political art, to which aspects of Adachi’s output also adhere, such as his early films Bowl (1961) and Closed Vagina (1963), which express the disillusionment of the 1960 security treaty protests through oblique metaphors like the titular female genitalia instead of more didactic messages. One of the many reasons a film like Galaxy (1967) is so engrossing and rewarding to rewatch is that you can read it as both an allegory of mid-’60s disenchantment and a surreal psychodrama about a bourgeois man’s mental breakdown. Far Weirder Than Just Agitprop Adachi’s more allegorical and ambiguous films may reward a closer look in ways the better-known ones — those in which the oppositional politics of the day are writ large — do not. Compared both to the militant documentaries of Shinsuke Ogawa, which chronicled the struggle of farmers opposed to the construction of Narita Airport in the 1960s and ’70s, and to the overtly political (and almost instructive) films of Jean-Luc Godard from around 1968 to 1976, much of Adachi’s work is far more opaque, even abstruse at times, despite the agitprop reputation of his output. Nominally a film about a notorious spree killer, A.K.A. Serial Killer is a highly conceptual exploration of state power residually haunting the postwar landscape of Japan, rendered through hypnotic visuals. Completed in 1969 but not shown publicly until 1975, it focuses on the everyday urban and rural spaces that shaped the perpetrator of sensational crimes and is regarded as a seminal work in landscape theory ( fūkeiron ). The Red Army/PFLP: Declaration of World War (1971), codirected with Wakamatsu, was filmed while Adachi was embedded among Palestinian guerrillas and was initially dismissed as merely recruitment propaganda for impressionable Japanese leftists, yet it is actually a pensive meditation on the nature of living on a daily basis as part of a revolutionary struggle, engaging in a dialectical inquiry with the viewer by posing questions and positions. Like. A.K.A. Serial Killer , Adachi’s recent films Revolution+1 (2022) and Escape (2025) have dealt with sensational figures — former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe’s assassin and the fugitive bomber Satoshi Kirishima, a marginal member of a group that carried out a series of bombings of corporations in the 1970s — albeit in a somewhat more conventional biopic style. Upon release, they prompted febrile responses in Japan (especially the Abe film), but the headlines overshadowed the fact these films were avowedly not celebrating their subjects. Neither condemning nor condoning, Revolution+1 portrays how Abe’s assassin was pulled almost inevitably toward his act by domestic and socioeconomic circumstances, while Escape focuses on the mental strain of living an ascetic life on the lam as a way of both atoning and continuing the struggle. In these times of endless culture wars and social divisions, such approaches to political art (and violence) are arguably more fertile than the didactic or provocative. An Artist’s Late Style Adachi has expressed admiration for Franz Kafka and Lu Xun, drawing on their writing for his film Artist of Fasting (2016), a typically bawdy tale of a man who arbitrarily takes up residence one day in a quiet neighborhood and becomes a spectacle attracting a broad range of people in society, all looking to exploit him for their agendas. Static, disjointed, and packed with literary references, the film seems very distant from Adachi’s 1960s and ’70s output’s cast of student activists and wannabe revolutionaries and its more frenetic pacing. And yet Artist of Fasting ultimately suggests a through line between both periods by functioning as an ironic portrait of an individual’s attempts to resist power. While the overtly politicized filmographies of others may date, Adachi’s oeuvre has the potential to outlive his and our lifetimes and offer lessons for future viewers. “Creating is, above of all, firstly about hoping,” Adachi wrote in 1970. Though his work lacks the formal elegance and stylistic consistency of Japanese filmmakers like Nagisa Ōshima ( Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence and In the Realm of the Senses ) and Yoshishige Yoshida ( Eros + Massacre ), it is precisely this anarchic range and rejection of cinematic convention that gives his cinema the capacity to retain political currency. And this should indeed give us hope.

articles.title: Treasury Market Volatility Is Capital Disciplining the State
articles.author: Stephen Maher
articles.content: Since the 2008 financial crisis, American economic policy has rested on the seemingly unshakable conviction that global markets for US government debt were bulletproof. This fact would supposedly allow the state to run enormous deficits indefinitely, financing massive tax cuts for the wealthy even while military spending approached $1 trillion. The same confidence underpinned the idea that the Federal Reserve possessed virtually unlimited firepower to contain economic crises. Yet in recent weeks, this assumption has begun to look considerably less secure. It turns out that even the American state is subject to the discipline of capital after all. As concerns over inflation mounted — and, perhaps more important, doubts about the willingness of the Fed to act to contain it grew — borrowing costs for the US state rose sharply. Last week, the ten-year Treasury rate crossed the symbolic threshold of 5 percent, its highest level since 2007. Although Donald Trump continued to loudly demand lower interest rates, the Fed saw little alternative but to raise them, while indicating that further hikes lie ahead. The move exposed the shortsightedness of suggestions that the era of central bank “independence” has come to an end. Indeed, the requirement that the Fed be able to impose monetary austerity regardless of electoral outcomes stems not merely from institutional rules or political culture but from the structural imperatives of capitalism itself. As Trump’s policies have run up against these constraints, his efforts to subordinate the Fed to his will have crumbled. Decline of the Petrodollar? Many will interpret this development as another step in the collapse of the American empire. Iran’s threats to sell oil in renminbi have led to prognostications about the imminent demise of the “petrodollar” regime, often depicted as the culmination of “de-dollarization” initiatives led especially by the BRICS. Yet the idea that the US empire rests on a “hydrocarbon-dollar complex” is a myth . The dollar’s status does not derive from the fact that any particular commodity is priced in dollars but from its role within the global credit system and the strength of the US economy. Large inflows of private investment into the United States have sustained demand for dollars, even as the dollar’s share of official reserve holdings has gradually declined. Moreover, that the dollar anchors credit markets means that the balance sheets of firms and central banks are tied to dollar obligations and assets. Debt is just as important — perhaps even more fundamental — for fueling global capitalism as fossil energy. To be sure, raising rates will have little impact on inflation — barring a truly drastic increase sufficient to spark a recession, as with the 1979 “Volcker Shock” that inaugurated the neoliberal period with an iron fist. Raising rates will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz and reverse the surge in oil prices now rippling through the economy. Nor can monetary policy undo Trump’s chaotic tariffs, which have also generated significant price pressures. Rather, the Fed’s imposition of monetary austerity is necessary to protect the stability of a global financial system that remains deeply dependent on the dollar. With enormous fiscal deficits requiring ever-growing issuance of Treasuries, failing to raise rates risked deepening the bond market sell-off by raising doubts about whether the Fed retained sufficient independence to impose discipline. Because the dollar is world money, this turmoil in Treasury markets would reverberate through credit, funding, and asset markets across the global economy. That the imposition of monetary austerity is necessary for global capitalism points to the illusory nature of the pro-worker Keynesian alternative imagined by some on the Left. The Fed was by no means faced with a straightforward choice between a pro-worker low-interest-rate policy and a pro-business high-interest-rate policy. Raising interest rates clearly has real costs for workers. On the other hand, had the Fed continued to pursue a more accommodative path, long-term US interest rates would likely have risen still further, increasing borrowing costs while threatening greater stress in Treasury markets. And a serious Treasury crisis — or the emergence of a “doom loop” in which the Fed became the dominant buyer of US debt — would hardly be good for workers. Given the existing balance of class forces, workers would doubtless bear the costs of restoring stability. Who Pays? Bond market volatility represents capital cracking down on the American state’s profligacy. The question now is who will pay for the belt-tightening. Rather than a lack of working-class discipline, at issue today is a macroeconomic regime that has combined tax cuts for capital and enormous military expenditures with war and tariffs. While Trump sought to partly fill the fiscal hole by aggressively slashing Medicaid, food assistance, and other programs for social provision, these cuts could only go so far. As inflation, rising interest costs, and volatility in Treasury markets narrow the room for maneuver, those priorities increasingly come into conflict. Either capital is made to absorb more of the adjustment through higher taxes and a reordering of fiscal priorities, or workers will be forced to pay through some combination of inflation, high interest rates, unemployment, and further cuts to social provision. The stakes extend beyond the affordability crisis. The same pressures that impose the need for adjustment also bear directly on the ability to address the existential crisis of climate change. Decarbonization requires enormous investments in energy, housing, transportation, and infrastructure over long time horizons, which are made much more difficult by growing pressure on public finances. Net interest payments have now surpassed military spending, exceeding $1 trillion per year, and are projected to rise rapidly as debt and borrowing costs increase. Yet it is impossible to imagine addressing the ecological crisis without massive expansion of state investment. Raising taxes, shifting budgetary priorities, and monetizing debt can create space to begin this project, but it would be a mistake to underestimate the extent to which capital will vehemently oppose all of this, let alone the extension of state planning a green transition would require. Achieving a sustainable future therefore hinges on building the power of the working class to take on capital and empire. While stabilizing Treasury markets is imperative in the short run to prevent a broader economic contraction and hold down household borrowing costs, the current turmoil demonstrates how sharply even the American state’s room to maneuver is circumscribed by financial markets. The episode reinforces the lessons drawn long ago by Marxist state theorists Ralph Miliband and Nicos Poulantzas: the capitalist state possesses real autonomy, but that autonomy remains decidedly relative. For socialists, the contradictions that follow from this fact cannot be escaped simply by choosing better monetary policies. This is precisely why the state cannot simply be wielded by socialists elected to govern it. The challenge, rather, is to operate within a state that is constrained by capitalism while simultaneously building the power necessary to transform those constraints — no small task.

articles.title: Zack Polanski’s Eco-Populism Could Do With More Socialism
articles.author: Chris Saltmarsh
articles.content: The Greens were for decades a relatively marginal force in British politics, with only one member of Parliament (MP) and a modest but growing number of local councilors. However, its prospects changed in September 2025 after Zack Polanski was elected party leader on an eco-populist platform. This new leadership defined itself against Labour Prime Minister Keir Starmer, rejecting his apologia for Israel’s genocide in Gaza as well as his fiscal austerity, anti-migrant measures, and anti-protest authoritarianism. Over the last year, the membership of the Green Party of England and Wales (there is a separate Scottish party) has surged from around 66,000 to over 230,000. This February, the Greens’ Hannah Spencer won the Gorton and Denton by-election, defeating both Labour and Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, and in May the Greens achieved their best-ever local election results. Now Polanski is running for Parliament in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election. In this contest, he aims not just to replace Starmer (who has resigned as an MP) but to consolidate the Greens’ position as a permanent left-wing opposition to the Labour Party. Polanski himself is unusual for the extent of his political development over a short timescale. In a new book, Russell Warfield describes how Polanski began his political career by joining the Liberal Democrats in 2015, toward the end of the party’s stint enacting austerity in coalition with the Conservatives. Polanski joined the Greens in 2017 after failing to be selected as a Lib Dem by-election candidate, all the while opposing Jeremy Corbyn’s leadership of the Labour Party from the right. Elected as a London Assembly member and deputy leader of the Greens, Polanski then moved to the left and defeated the more centrist incumbents in last year’s leadership election. In this context, Warfield’s book The Green Socialist: Zack Polanski and the Battle for Britain’s Future book is a timely contribution to understanding the Green Party as it seeks to forge a new role in British politics. Warfield is transparent about his own political commitments. A long-standing left-wing Green Party member, he volunteered on Polanski’s leadership campaign and sees the party as a vehicle for ecosocialism. The Green Socialist is thus most useful as an insight into how Polanski’s most erudite supporters think of themselves, their project, and the man currently at its center. Optimism flows through Warfield’s analysis, but the book is also a productive entry point for considering the challenges facing the Green Party in the current political environment. While the inconsistency of Polanski’s politics may represent a genuine personal journey, it also underpins latent incoherences within the project associated with his leadership. Polanski has inspired hope so far because he effectively reflects back to his supporters the political and moral principles that they already hold. This apparent attempt to rerun Corbyn’s Labour leadership has drawn support both from prominent figures and dedicated activists from that period, as well as a new generation not forged by that experience. For this project to succeed, they must now collectively reckon with the current incoherence of the Greens’ electoral strategy, political offer, and party organization. Optimism While Warfield echoes some Green members’ calls for a new focus on “community organizing” (a vague ambition that has both preoccupied and evaded much of the British left for several years), Polanski’s leadership continues to define success in terms of electoral victories. His distinct strategy has been to maximize the party’s potential with an eco-populist political offer and more sophisticated communications. Warfield embraces the necessarily difficult task of analyzing such an electoral project while it is not just ongoing but still in its very early stages. The book went to print before the Makerfield by-election, which resulted in Andy Burnham’s return to the House of Commons as a Labour MP and his successful ouster of Starmer as prime minister. This means that now very significant context is out of scope in the analysis. Without doubt, Polanski’s bid to reach Parliament in the coming Holborn and St Pancras by-election will itself be a defining chapter in this story. Such accounts are thus inevitably provisional and partial, and Warfield is right to historicize Polanski’s rise in order to give the reader a stronger basis for understanding events as they continue to occur. Working backward, he locates the Polanski project in a lineage of electoral advances and leftward shifts in the Greens’ recent past. This particularly includes Natalie Bennett and Caroline Lucas’s spells as leader, as well as an ecosocialist tradition in the party dating back to the mid-2000s. However, this optimistic story of the Greens’ initially slow and steady but now accelerating advance is complicated by recent events. Burnham’s arrival as prime minister makes Polanski’s task more difficult, as he seeks to differentiate himself from an apparently authentic and relatively popular Labour leader who is prepared to criticize neoliberalism. This challenge was underlined by the Greater Manchester mayoral by-election on July 30, which Labour won decisively despite the Greens’ hubristic claims that they alone could defeat the hard-right Reform. A Polanski defeat in Holborn and St Pancras would not signal an end to his project. Yet in further slowing the Greens’ momentum, it would raise questions about whether the party can adapt to the new terrain under his leadership. Purpose A Polanski victory in Holborn and St Pancras, on the other hand, would likely renew the party’s confidence that it can win anywhere, especially to damage the Labour government from the left. Still, even such an outcome should not obscure the deeper incoherence that has underlain the Greens’ current electoral strategy. Within Warfield’s account, we can identify three distinct electoral aims expressed in the party: to supplant Labour; to stop Reform UK; and to represent a progressive social bloc. Polanski is quoted in The Green Socialist as aiming to replace Labour as the main party of the Left. In this vision, the Greens see themselves as capitalizing on a broader realignment in British politics, with the old parties in terminal decline. However, this trend is less obvious today than it appeared a year ago. Just as Farage’s Reform UK has struggled to fully supplant the Conservatives, Labour has consolidated its position by substituting the uniquely out-of-touch Starmer with Burnham’s centrist populism. This strategy mobilizes Burnham’s Northern English identity and working-class affect against the Westminster system, while offering piecemeal ameliorations to the cost-of-living crisis. Polanski has, for now, lost his monopoly on hope in British politics, meaning he is no longer able to just fill the space abandoned by Labour. Reaching beyond his natural supporters to build a diverse social coalition motivated to support his eco-populist insurgency is a more compromising task. This tumultuous political environment further complicates the second thrust of the Greens’ electoral mission: the call to stop Farage and his Reform UK vehicle. While the Gorton and Denton by-election demonstrated the Greens’ capacity to play this role, other parties have shown they can too. As well as Labour retaining the Greater Manchester mayoralty, Plaid Cymru cohered the anti-Reform bloc in last year’s Caerphilly by-election. Furthermore, beyond specific (by-)elections, Labour has the strongest claim to the anti-Reform mantel nationally, as the only party that can plausibly incorporate both Green and Reform voters into its own coalition. Indeed, although both the Greens and Reform are motivated by an antiestablishment energy, both lack a genuinely majoritarian impulse; they each appeal to distinct social bases that are highly unlikely to vote for the other in great numbers. This puts a relatively low ceiling of support on both parties. The Greens’ third electoral purpose, the least explicitly discussed by Warfield, thus appears to be the most viable. Labour may be the strongest electoral bulwark against the far right, but the Greens can confidently claim to be the main political opposition. While Burnham continues to tail Reform with regressive migration policies and backsliding on climate action, Polanski’s Greens can differentiate themselves as the standard-bearers of migrants’ rights, climate justice, and anti-fascist and Palestine solidarity. By consistently offering a principled alternative to Reform in the public debate, the Greens could secure a permanent place on the Left of British politics without indulging in the compromises required for outright electoral victory. Ecosocialism It is evident in Warfield’s account, though, that sections of Polanski’s supporters are not satisfied with a party that simply reflects progressive talking points back to a minority section of voters. Warfield, like the party faction Greens Organise (composed mostly of activists not schooled in Corbynism), is committed to an ecosocialist politics. Even though Warfield projects the label onto Polanski (including in the book’s title), Polanski prefers to describe himself as an eco-populist. In fact, I could find no public record of Polanski proactively using the term ecosocialist. This exposes a contradiction within not just the Green Party but the Polanski project itself. This distinction between eco-populism and ecosocialism is not just semantic. For it also represents a latent tension between Polanski as the figure who has catalyzed the Greens’ rise and more politically ambitious elements of his base. If ecosocialism is an ideological politics (socialism within ecological limits, per Warfield), then eco-populism is a communication strategy (the construction of a “people” mobilized against a socio-ecological enemy, as in the call to support the 99 percent against the ultraelite 1 percent). Although they may be complementary, the one does not necessarily imply the other. Polanski’s use of eco-populism is relatively unsophisticated, deployed to signal an implicit environmentalism while mostly speaking about inequality. Ecosocialism is laden with a greater depth of meaning, however. Warfield characterizes this as a project to build the economy within ecological limits, by discarding both the profit motive and the pursuit of perpetual growth. This implies an essentially revolutionary politics of rupture with the core logics of capitalism, even if Green ecosocialists don’t necessarily articulate it in that register. This is not to say that ecosocialists should adopt the style of unreconstructed revolutionaries. But it is necessary to politically clarify the contradictions between socio-ecological transition and capitalism, especially considering the urgent timescales of the climate crisis. Ecosocialism simultaneously implies both a conviction regarding what must be done and uncertainty about how to achieve it, amid an unprecedented constellation of structural crises. It means offering a programmatic alternative to a growth strategy based on the combination of remilitarization, artificial intellgience, and fossil fuel production — a socio-ecologically destructive strategy to which Burnham’s Labour still subscribes. If the Greens’ current political approach is a shopping list of more or less agreeable (and sometimes contradictory) left-wonkish policies, ecosocialism implies a shift toward a program of democratic ecological planning and experiments in transition. Organization For Green ecosocialists serious about this politics, the key question is whether the party’s organizational structure is currently capable of developing and advancing this alternative. The answer, quite manifestly, is no. Warfield argues in The Green Socialist that the main point of optimism is not Polanski himself but the party’s membership and democratic structures. While this is a useful corrective against a tendency to overinvest in inevitably inadequate leaders, it underplays the limitations of the party’s democracy and culture. Currently, the Greens have a structure that allows any member to attend party conferences and vote on policy motions. While this may appear to be participatory, it only aggregates individual preferences rather than cultivating a collective democracy. Those who self-select to determine Green Party policy experience no democratic accountability, and those who cannot attend conferences have no opportunity to shape their political composition. This is not the mass deliberation needed in order to develop a shared analysis and a coherent ecosocialist program to drive the project forward. Furthermore, the lack of a democratic whip for councilors or MPs means that they are free to ignore the party membership or prioritize local concerns over advancing collective priorities. The composition of Greens Organise means that it has not learned the most important lesson from Corbyn’s Labour. Like previously failed projects on the Left, the faction has deprioritized organizational questions rather than understanding that satisfactorily resolving them is a precondition for sustained outward-facing success. But Green ecosocialists must be prepared to confront the limitations of the party. Its democratic structures are not something to be celebrated but completely remade in service of a collective party life.
